title: Banijay Kids & Family Sells ’Little Princess’ to Sky U.K.(EXCLUSIVE)
description: “Little Princess,” the British pre-school animation classic, is heading to Sky UK, in a deal struck with Banijay Kids & Family which sees the pay T
body:
“Little Princess,” the British pre-school animation classic, is heading to Sky UK, in a deal struck with Banijay Kids & Family which sees the pay TV buying its complete catalog.

	Further new distribution deals on “Little Princess,” a four-time BAFTA nominee, have been struck with Nordisk Film, RTV Slovenia and Italy’s TIM.

	Based on the best-selling children’s books by award-winning author and illustrator Tony Ross, “Little Princess” launched on the U.K.’s Channel 4 “Milkshake” children’s TV block in 2006 and ran through four seasons of a total 135 episodes, the last ending in 2020.
	

	First time round, when on linear TV, “Little Princess” was released in 140 territories. The deal announced by Banijay Kids & Family on Wednesday at Mipcom o underscore that what the market is looking for is evergreen brands, not necessarily brand new linear TV shows.


	“Little Princess” has, however, cultivated from 2008 to a fandom base on YouTube and other platforms, underscoring its resilient appeal.

	Sky U.K. has acquired all series and specials. Nordisk Film has acquired Seasons 1-3 and the series’ specials for SVOD across the Nordics; RTV Slovenia has Seasons 1-2, and Telecom Italia’s TIM for its Italian streaming platform aggregator, TIMVision.

	“Little Princess” is produced by The Illuminated Film Company, also behind Eric Carle’s “The Very Hungry Caterpillar and Other Stories” and the RTS Award winning “The Rubbish World of Dave Spud.”

	Set in a comfy world of gentle blocked colors, an ever blue sky, lovely grass low hills stretching to the horizon, and a purple-bricked castle, “Little Princess” turns on the antics of the bubbly, ever inquisitive and endearing titular character.
	

	Sporting a permanent yellow crown teeth and craggy mild teeth who confronts every day problems – such as getting a scratch after a very minor accident on “I Need a Plaster. Coddled by her parents and the cast service, she learns, however, that she might be a princess but won’t always get her own way. Each episode, as Banijay Friends & Family notes, is told with a warm blend of humor and surprise.

	“Across the industry, we’re seeing continued demand for trusted, established IP that can cut through in an increasingly crowded landscape. With a new U.K. home on Sky and partners across Europe, ‘Little Princess’ demonstrates the enduring value of distinctive characters and storytelling that audiences know and love,” said Julia Rowlands, SVP Sales, Co-Productions and Acquisitions, Banijay Kids & Family.Led by CEO Benoît Di Sabatino, Banijay Kids & Family brings together leading production companies – Monello Productions, Movimenti Production, Procidis, Tiger Aspect Kids & Family, Zodiak Kids & Family France, and Zodiak Productions UK – spanning France, Italy, and the U.K.

	It is behind preeminent kids’ brands including “Totally Spies!,” “Mr Bean,” “Once Upon a Time…, LoliRock,” “Super Happy Magic Forest,” “Street Football” and “MiniHeroes of the Forest.”

schema.headline: Banijay Kids & Family Sells ’Little Princess’ to Sky U.K.(EXCLUSIVE)

title: Edinburgh Film Festival Reveals Dates for 2027 Edition (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
The Edinburgh International Film Festival has announced the dates for its 80th edition, set to run Aug. 12-18, 2027.

	Supported by Screen Scotland
body:
The Edinburgh International Film Festival has announced the dates for its 80th edition, set to run Aug. 12-18, 2027.

	Supported by Screen Scotland, the milestone edition will honour the festival’s long history while building on the success of its revitalised iteration, launched in 2024 under the leadership of CEO and festival director Paul Ridd and festival producer Emma Boa. Submissions open in Jan. 2027.


	The 2026 edition featured a programme made up of 60% world premieres, which played out in four venues across the city, and boasted a 35% increase in admissions on 2025. Among the highlights was a sold-out “Trainspotting” anniversary event at Leith Theatre with live commentary from the production team, including stars Ewan McGregor and Ewan Bremner, and a club night DJ’d by Irvine Welsh and Darren Emerson, as well as the inaugural U.K. Film Conference which included a keynote from BFI CEO Ben Roberts.
	

	In 2027 the film festival also joins Edinburgh Festival Fringe and Edinburgh International Festival in celebrating eight decades of creativity and bringing audiences together in the Scottish capital.

	“We are beyond excited to celebrate our fourth edition as the revamped and revitalised festival in August next year, as well as 80 years of EIFF. This is a major milestone in the story of our historic Festival, and we intend to do this anniversary justice with an exciting range of films, events and unforgettable moments in our beautiful city,” said Ridd.

	“World premieres remain a huge priority for us as do our competitions, as we bring fresh and exciting films to audiences, industry and press. We are committed to engaging with the next generation of talent as well as established voices, providing a curated and commercial platform for work to be celebrated and found. Over the coming months we will be opening up submissions, and continuing our close dialogue with the film and screen industries, building on the successes of our 2026 edition to continue to make EIFF a place where the future of filmmaking is not simply discussed, but actively shaped. Bring it on.”

schema.headline: Edinburgh Film Festival Reveals Dates for 2027 Edition (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Russell T Davies Calls BBC Boss’ AI ‘Doctor Who’ Comment ‘Clumsy’ and Teases Show’s Future: ‘You’ll Start to See Production’ in ‘Summer Next Year’
description: Outgoing “Doctor Who” showrunner Russell T. Davies has criticised BBC director general Matt Brittin over recent comments he made regarding an AI-ge
body:
Outgoing “Doctor Who” showrunner Russell T. Davies has criticised BBC director general Matt Brittin over recent comments he made regarding an AI-generated episode of the cult show. 

	Speaking at the Royal Television Society conference last month, Brittin said he’d been sent a fully AI-generated episode of “Doctor Who,” which he described as “pretty good.” Although he was quick to add it was “not going to replace humans,” his wording sparked instant criticism, and Brittin later admitted he had “got into trouble” over what he’d said. Now one of the biggest names in “Doctor Who” has spoken up. 
	

	“That’s a clumsy thing to say in an industry where he’s got writers and artists and it specifically affects people, they’re the first to take the blow,” said Davies, speaking to BBC Radio 4’s The Media Show. “My inbox went ping ping ping ping ping, so God knows what his was like.”


	Davies — who revived “Doctor Who” in 2005 and then returned again in 2023 — also said that Brittin, who only recently joined the BBC following a career at Google, “hasn’t worked in television for that long and might not be so fruity with an opinion in future.”

	The future of “Doctor Who” — a BBC icon for more than 60 years — is currently up in the air following the departure of Disney+ as a co-financier. This summer, Davies announced he would be stepping back and the BBC cancelled the planned Christmas special. Last month, the BBC launched a competitive tender inviting pitches from producers to reboot the series. “Line of Duty” creator Jed Mercurio is among those to have submitted their interest. 
	

	But while fans wait to see what happens, Davies, despite no longer being involved in the show, assured that a new series was definitely happening and there wouldn’t be too long to wait. 

	“You’ll start to see production with a brand-new Doctor, a brand-new companion, summer next year,” he said.

schema.headline: Russell T Davies Calls BBC Boss’ AI ‘Doctor Who’ Comment ‘Clumsy’ and Teases Show’s Future: ‘You’ll Start to See Production’ in ‘Summer Next Year’

title: Todd Haynes on Pedro Pascal-Led ‘De Noche,’ What You Can’t See on Screen and the Radical Power of Love
description: LYON, France — When Mexican costume designer Anna Terrazas told Todd Haynes that the most important thing about a costume was what it smelled like,
body:
LYON, France — When Mexican costume designer Anna Terrazas told Todd Haynes that the most important thing about a costume was what it smelled like, the filmmaker had just one response: “You’re hired.”

	The Oscar-nominated director shared the anecdote about his upcoming Pedro Pascal-starring romantic noir drama “De Noche” at the Lumière Film Festival on Tuesday, offering a glimpse into his approach to filmmaking, from the music and sounds that shape his movies to the senses that cannot always be expressed on screen.
	

	“We see movies with our ears and our eyes,” Haynes explained. “But movies that evoke smell and touch and other kinds of senses are the ones that keep allowing us to fill in.”


	Haynes is in Lyon with longtime producer Christine Vachon for a retrospective featuring four of his films: “Poison,” “Safe,” “Far From Heaven” and “I’m Not There,” including newly restored versions of the first two.

	The director – whose latest film follows the story of a detective (Pascal) and a younger schoolteacher (Danny Ramirez) who flee the corruption of 1930s Los Angeles for Mexico – described the homework he sets himself before each production. He said he immerses himself in films that share its genre or cinematic style, rather than necessarily its historical setting.

	“It’s as if I give myself an assignment each time,” he said, explaining how that research feeds into what he calls his “image books,” which he shares with his collaborators.

	While putting together the image book for his Oscar-nominated “May December,” starring frequent collaborator Julianne Moore alongside Natalie Portman, Haynes began listening to Michel Legrand‘s score for Joseph Losey’s “The Go-Between.”
	

	The music soon became central to the project. He played it on set from the very first day, using it to choreograph camera movements. By the editing stage, the music had become so integral to the film that Haynes asked composer Marcelo Zarvos to rearrange and adapt it. “We couldn’t let it go,” he recalled. “It became a definitive part of the structure, the language, and the energy of the film.”

	Having watched the restored version of “Safe” the previous evening in Lyon, Haynes praised sound designer Leslie Shatz for the unsettling soundscape of the 1995 drama, in which Moore plays a woman suffering from a mysterious illness.

	He described “all of the strange, lurking, unconscious sounds” in the film, that created what he called “a kind of magnetic field in which the contamination she senses from her surroundings becomes literally audible.”

	Turning to his six-time Oscar-nominated 2015 romance “Carol,” Haynes recalled how journalists kept congratulating him and stars Cate Blanchett and Cannes Best Actress winner Rooney Mara for portraying strong women. Blanchett, he said, would object: Carol wasn’t some invincible heroine but a woman constrained by her time, struggling to understand herself and how she wanted to live.

	“There is something radical and anti-social about love,” Haynes said, citing great French writer Roland Barthes’ “A Lover’s Discourse,” passages of which he shared with the actors.

	Haynes also paid tribute to Vachon, who helped rescue “Safe” when he was struggling to raise its $1 million budget. The film, he said, wouldn’t exist without her.

	Vachon, who already had a grasp of the industry’s commercial realities, recalled the practical advice she gave him years earlier when he proposed making his first feature, “Poison” as three interconnected 20-minute stories.

	“I said, you know what, Todd? Make it 90 minutes,” she recalled.

	The producer made some pointed observations about the state of independent cinema. She sees younger Americans flocking to repertory theaters, including her own 26-year-old daughter, but worries about what the industry is offering them.

	“I feel like we are creating a new generation of cinemagoers, but we’re just not giving them enough movies to see,” she said.
	

	Haynes also revisited his childhood obsession with Lucille Ball, which inspired his autobiographical short “Dottie Gets Spanked.” He went on to tease a possible screening of the film alongside “Superstar: The Karen Carpenter Story,” his cult short made with Barbie dolls that has rarely been shown publicly since legal disputes over its music rights. The filmmaker was hinting heavily at what might be in store for the festival’s surprise screening Wednesday evening at the Institut Lumière.

	The Lumière Film Festival runs in Lyon through Oct. 18.

schema.headline: Todd Haynes on Pedro Pascal-Led ‘De Noche,’ What You Can’t See on Screen and the Radical Power of Love

title: Philippine-Italian Sales Alliance Targets Indie Film Buyers in Asia, Europe and North America (EXCLUSIVE)
description: A new Philippine-Italian sales alliance aims to put independent films in front of buyers in Asia, Europe and North America. Fire & Ice Media, the P
body:
A new Philippine-Italian sales alliance aims to put independent films in front of buyers in Asia, Europe and North America. Fire & Ice Media, the Philippine producer and sales agent, and Italy’s Coccinelle Film Sales unveiled the strategic partnership at Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market.

	The pair will work together on a handpicked group of films, combining their regional know-how and buyer contacts to seek distribution deals beyond the films’ home markets. A first batch of films has already been chosen, though the companies have yet to name them.
	

	Abell Diño-Cabrera, who heads Fire & Ice Media and runs the division’s film and TV development, production, positioning and sales work, will steer the alliance for the Philippine side.


	“Every film has its own audience and its own potential in different markets. Our job is to understand where those opportunities are and work with the right people to make them happen,” said Diño-Cabrera. “Partnering with Coccinelle allows us to strengthen our reach, share market knowledge, and create more possibilities for the filmmakers and producers who trust us to represent their work.”

	Coccinelle, set up by Francesca Breccia, sells independent titles on the international circuit, pairing films and their rights owners with buyers and distributors in a range of territories. Breccia said the company already had sales alliances with Asian counterparts, notably in South Korea and Thailand, and was delighted to now bring the Philippines into that network.

	“Filipino cinema has a strong identity and remarkable creative energy, with stories and voices that deserve greater international exposure. I was particularly drawn to Fire & Ice Media’s lineup, which combines a distinctive arthouse sensibility with strong commercial potential,” Breccia said. “I look forward to joining forces and creating new opportunities for independent films across international markets.”
	

	Fire & Ice was at the Asian Contents & Film Market with a slate of Filipino titles. On offer are Phil Giordano’s “Bilyarista,” a sports drama with a female lead; Nigel Santos’ queer ensemble piece “Open Endings”; David R. Corpuz’s “Only Known to Us”; Law Fajardo’s “The Hearing”; and “Crosspoint,” a Philippines-Japan thriller from Donie Ordiales. A selection of films by Brillante Mendoza rounds out the lineup.

	Several international co-productions and development projects are also in the works. Among them are Mendoza’s “Aid,” Ham Tran’s supernatural thriller “Red Thread” and “Karaoke News,” a crime thriller from John Paul Su that takes aim at the media.

	Parent company Fire & Ice Entertainment, co-founded by CEO Liza Diño and Ice Seguerra, spans film and TV production, international sales, music, live events and creative consultancy. Its Media arm has been a partner on international co-productions such as Nicole Midori Woodford’s “Last Shadow at First Light,” which bowed in San Sebastián in 2023, and Matsubayashi Urara’s “Blue Imagine,” a 2024 Rotterdam premiere.

	The company’s homegrown projects include “Never the Bride,” a scripted drama series from Diño about a wedding planner whose own marriage is falling apart, and “Funeral Flowers,” a family drama feature she will write and direct. Seguerra is attached to direct “Alex & Rio,” a road movie driven by music.

	Diño said the company had learned over the years that a robust slate is merely the starting point.

	“Every market is different. Buyers have their own interests, audiences have different tastes, and sometimes a film finds its opportunity through a conversation with the right person who understands what it has to offer,” she said. “That’s what makes this collaboration with Coccinelle meaningful to us. We bring different strengths, relationships, and knowledge of our respective markets. But ultimately, we share the same goal: to serve the films we represent, find the right partners who believe in them, and give these stories the best possible opportunity to reach audiences. We see this as the beginning of a meaningful long-term relationship.”

schema.headline: Philippine-Italian Sales Alliance Targets Indie Film Buyers in Asia, Europe and North America (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Judge Extends Block on Trump’s White House Ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico
description: Following President Donald Trump‘s White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico last month, a federal judge has once again blocked him from doing so
body:
Following President Donald Trump‘s White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico last month, a federal judge has once again blocked him from doing so.

	U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly wrote in the ruling issued Tuesday evening that the outlets are “likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two First Amendment claims.” Thus, the Court granted their motion for a preliminary injunction and extended the previously awarded relief, which will continue to preserve the status quo as the case proceeds.
	

	“Still, no one should interpret the Court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed,” the judge noted. 


	The judge previously ordered the White House to immediately reinstate access to the news organizations on Sept. 24 after the president banned them initially. At the time, Kelly granted the news orgs’ motion for a temporary restraining order in their lawsuit against Trump and three White House officials, alleging the ban violated the First Amendment.

	The White House must “immediately return, reinstate, and restore the White House ‘hard pass’ press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO that were revoked on or about September 18, 2026, until further Order of the Court or the expiration of this Temporary Restraining Order,” Kelly wrote in the ruling. 

	In September, Trump posted on social media that he was “proud to announce that, effective immediately,” he was “banning” the three outlets from the White House. When reporters from those news organizations arrived the following day, they were denied entry despite holding “hard passes.” CNN, MS NOW and Politico then sued Trump and three White House officials over the ban, alleging it violates the First Amendment and “brazenly discriminates based on editorial viewpoint.”

schema.headline: Judge Extends Block on Trump’s White House Ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico

title: Going Big in Japan: International French Hit ‘Bright Minds’ Season 7 Heads to Tokyo (EXCLUSIVE)
description: The latest season of French hit “Bright Minds” marks a major milestone for France TV Distribution’s light crime series, with part of the filming ta
body:
The latest season of French hit “Bright Minds” marks a major milestone for France TV Distribution’s light crime series, with part of the filming taking place in Tokyo for the first time due to its huge popularity in the country.

	The unprecedented co-production between JLA Productions and NHK Enterprises of Japan was made possible thanks to France TV Distribution, which played a key role as a business facilitator and matchmaker in bringing together the two companies. 
	

	The collaboration opens new perspectives for the series and strengthens its international reach, according to the Paris-based world sales company.


	“Bright Minds” (known in France as “Astrid et Raphaëlle”), about a neurodivergent police records archivist with an extraordinary memory and perspicacity who assists an impulsive police inspector solve complex crimes, has established itself as the most-watched series in France. In 2025, the show accumulated 24 million video views on france.tv, making it the most-watched scripted series on the platform (excluding daytime).

	Season 7 promises to take Astrid (Sara Mortensen) and Raphaëlle (Lola Dewaere) through a slew of new adventures and personal challenges, from survivalism and ancient Egypt to Hindu communities, houseboat murders and investigations between Paris and Tokyo. 

	Astrid and Raphaëlle have their work cut out for them as their daily lives are suddenly turned upside down: the police records department is threatened with closure, abruptly depriving Astrid of her bearings as she faces the loss of her one and only refuge. Raphaëlle, meanwhile, is recovering after a long rehabilitation and must confront the loss of her mobility, which prevents her from conducting investigations with her former energy.
	

	To face these new challenges, Astrid and Raphaëlle are forced to completely reinvent their relationship, potentially threatening their precious friendship.

	Astrid and Raphaëlle are at the heart of the series’ success, which extends far beyond French borders: “Bright Minds” has sold in more than 130 countries and its popularity continues to grow. The series has also inspired a British remake, the Channel 4 hit “Patience,” as well as the new Spanish show “Ágata and Lola.”

	The original show’s international profile has now been further bolstered by its shoot in Japan, where the series has become such a huge hit that setting part of Season 7 in Tokyo was a natural next step.

	“For several years, we had dreamed of filming episodes of ‘Bright Minds’ in Tokyo,” said Jean-Sébastien Bouilloux, producer at JLA Productions. “Thanks to France Télévisions, France TV Distribution and NHK Enterprises Inc., that dream became a reality for Season 7.”

	In 2025, France TV Distribution organized a major promotional tour in Tokyo for the team, including press conferences and fan meetings, illustrating the exceptional enthusiasm ‘Bright Minds’ generates in Japan. Season 1 of the series premiered in Japan in 2021 on the cable and satellite outlet Mystery Channel (then AXN Mystery), and subsequently aired on public broadcaster NHK starting in 2022. All six seasons to date have aired on both broadcasters, with catch-up streaming also attracted high viewing figures and outperforming many other programs, according to France TV Distribution. 

	With each new season, the series has expanded its audience base across both broadcast and streaming platforms, and this popularity has also translated into steady DVD sales. When the cast visited Japan in March 2025, Mystery Channel hosted a special event attended by 270 lucky fans chosen from applicants nationwide, giving them the opportunity to meet and interact with the cast.

	Premiering in February 2026 on Mystery Channel, Season 6 achieved the highest ratings ever recorded for the series on J:COM, Japan’s largest cable TV operator.

	Season 7 and the two episodes filmed in Japan mark “a real turning point in the life of the series,” Bouilloux added, expressing confidence that they would “both surprise and delight audiences in both countries.”
	

	“This is the first time ‘Bright Minds’ has gone abroad,” Bouilloux noted. “It is also the first recurring French series to do so, and I am very proud that it happened in Japan, a country with which the series has had many connections since its creation.”

	“The shoot was a wonderful adventure, especially in the collaboration between the French and Japanese crews, and above all an incredible source of creativity and fruitful exchanges. The JLA and France TV Distribution teams worked hand in hand throughout the entire production process to bring this new season to life.”

	The co-production also proved a positive experience for producers at NHK. 

	“From the very beginning, I was struck by the team’s sincere desire to embrace Japanese culture with authenticity and respect, said Koji Sakabe of NHK Enterprises. “That spirit made this collaboration truly meaningful.”

	Julia Schulte, head of international sales at France TV Distribution, added: “We are truly grateful to our partners at JLA and NHK Enterprises Inc., as well as to our colleagues at France Télévisions and all the incredible talents involved.

	“Their open-mindedness, creativity, and enthusiasm made this new Franco-Japanese adventure possible. We are delighted to have set up the first co-production between our companies, and we hope it will be the first of many more to come.”

	Created by Alexandre de Seguins and Laurent Burtin, “Bright Minds” is directed by Jérôme Alméras and Amandine Bonnin. The series is produced by JLA Productions for France Télévisions.

	In addition to Mortensen and Dewaere, the cast includes Benoît Michel, Sophia Yamna, Jean-Louis Garçon, Husky Kihal, Jean-Benoît Souilh, Kengo Saïto and Charlotte Gaccio.

schema.headline: Going Big in Japan: International French Hit ‘Bright Minds’ Season 7 Heads to Tokyo (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ORF-Enterprise Boards ‘Crème de la Crème’ – About a Sperm Bank Business – Produced by Whatever Pictures and a ‘Playful and Irreverent’ Series
description: Finnish production company Whatever Pictures has signed a new global sales deal with ORF-Enterprise, part of Austrian braodcaster ORF, which has ac
body:
Finnish production company Whatever Pictures has signed a new global sales deal with ORF-Enterprise, part of Austrian braodcaster ORF, which has acquired international distribution rights to the comedy drama “Crème de la Crème.”

	Commissioned domestically by Finnish broadcaster YLE, the show is written and directed by showrunner Jukka Vidgrén, Topi Koljonen, Henna Rinnekangas, Juuso Laatio and Anna Heinämaa. Vidgrén and Antti Kaarlela produce.
	

	It follows Joonas, a young farmer, who lives on his childhood dairy farm and takes pride in the rural lifestyle. He enjoys the work, but the farm is on the brink of collapse, with no clear future in sight. That is until he sets up a booming sperm bank business with the help of his friends.


	Armin Luttenberger, Head of Content Sales International at ORF-Enterprise, noted that it is the “Finnish identity” of the show that makes it distinctive.

	“Still, the underlying themes are highly universal: ambition, economic pressure, friendship and the question of how far you are willing to go to secure your future. It feels very local without being culturally closed, which is often a strong combination for international audiences,” he said.

	It’s not exactly what most viewers would expect from the Nordics.

	“Yes, and that is one of its strengths. Nordic drama is still often associated internationally with crime, darker tones and a certain visual restraint. ‘Crème de la Crème’ brings a much more playful and irreverent energy. It is still unmistakably Nordic in its setting and sensibility, but it shows a different, more humorous side of the region.”
	

	That doesn’t mean that crime doesn’t pay anymore. 

	At Mipcom, Whatever Pictures presented “Three Fires,” a border thriller set in North Karelia, and “Ice House,” an international assassin thriller co-written by Marteinn Thorisson and Puranen.

	The company is also joining forces with Norway’s Rein Film on the new scripted crime series “Silent Herd,” currently in development.

	Set in a contemporary Sápmi community – during the polar night – it shows an investigator who is forced to return to the village they fled in their youth after a traumatic childhood marked by bullying and exclusion.

	“When suspicious deaths begin to expose old wounds within a powerful reindeer-herding family, the investigation becomes both a murder mystery and a personal reckoning,” said producer Aleksi Puranen.

	“We want the series to be gripping and atmospheric, but also more specific than a traditional Nordic noir. The landscape, the darkness, the family histories, the silence of the community and the pressure of unresolved trauma are all part of the storytelling.”

	Rein Films’ Mathis Ståhle Mathisen explained that the collaboration felt “very natural” – for several reasons.

	“Firstly, Sápmi is a region that extends across national borders, including both Norway and Finland, so a Finnish-Norwegian collaboration is a logical creative and production choice for a story rooted in that world.”

	Secondly, Whatever Pictures and Rein Film had already worked together on “A Midnight Sun Affair.”

	“We discovered that the two companies share similar ambitions: to tell stories from the North with authenticity, strong local voices and international ambition. ‘The Silent Herd’ felt like the natural next step.”

	They will once again be working with director Ken Are Bongo and writer Jens Martin Mienna.

	According to Kaarlela, the Sápmi world, its language, land, family, reindeer herding, sense of belonging and silence are all integral to the story.

	“At the same time, we’re very aware that this world must be approached with care. We are not looking at the Sámi community from the outside. Key creatives on the project, including Ken Are Bongo and Jens Martin Mienna, are Sámi themselves, and we are developing the series closely with them. As with ‘A Midnight Sun Affair,’ we carefully follow Sámi guidelines and cultural protocols.”
	

	Fittingly for a crime thriller, the series explores “darker human territory: violence, shame, revenge and power within a small community.” But these are not presented as “Sámi traits,” he emphasized.

	“They are the dramatic territory of the genre, explored through specific Sámi characters and a specific Sápmi setting. The important thing for us is that the world is truthful, the authorship is connected to the community, and the characters are people first.”

schema.headline: ORF-Enterprise Boards ‘Crème de la Crème’ – About a Sperm Bank Business – Produced by Whatever Pictures and a ‘Playful and Irreverent’ Series

title: Tallinn-Bound Indian Drama ‘Kidney’ Boarded by Shiladitya Bora’s Platoon One Films (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Indian drama “Kidney,” the second feature from filmmaking siblings Aakarsh and Agrim Sansanwal, has been boarded by Shiladitya Bora’s Platoon One F
body:
Indian drama “Kidney,” the second feature from filmmaking siblings Aakarsh and Agrim Sansanwal, has been boarded by Shiladitya Bora’s Platoon One Films, which joins as co-producer ahead of the film’s slot in the Critics’ Picks Competition at Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF).

	The film is produced by Enfant Terrible Productions, the Mumbai outfit the brothers set up. Set in an isolated Indian village, it follows a young man and woman from feuding families who fall in love. When a quarrel over an inheritance revives old hostilities, their relationship comes under pressure from greed and treachery in a conflict not of their making.
	

	“We made the film with very little money and a seemingly inexhaustible supply of spirit,” said Aakarsh Sansanwal. “When the budget ran out, the entire village, its farming community, stood behind us. They helped us through the hurdles and, in their own way, became part of the film’s journey. This film carries the hands and hearts of the people who helped bring it into the world.”


	“Kidney” adds to a Platoon One slate that counts “Bayaan,” “Toh Ti Ani Fuji,” “Bhagwan Bharose,” “Minimum,” “Ghaath,” “Picasso” and “Yours Truly” among its titles.

	The director said Platoon One was among the first to spot that spirit in the film and back what the brothers were attempting. “Their support gave the film a chance to travel beyond the world in which it was made and reach audiences we could only have hoped for. To see it now receive recognition and find its way into the light is deeply moving. My thanks to the Tallinn Black Nights team for discovering our film and giving it a place to shine.”
	

	Tallinn’s Critics’ Picks strand spotlights films with a clear artistic point of view and a fresh take on storytelling, including work that wrestles with genre, cinema’s past and the social issues of the moment. Earlier selections include Arati Kadav’s “Mrs.,” starring Sanya Malhotra, as well as “The Brothers Kitaura,” “About Us But Not About Us” and “The Bone Breakers.”

	Bora, who founded Platoon One, said that when he first watched “Kidney” he knew he was “looking at something different, something that hadn’t been attempted in quite this way.” He also pointed to the Sansanwals’ “strong and distinct voice.”

	“It would be easy to dismiss a film like ‘Kidney’ as esoteric, but what struck me was the depth of emotion underneath its craft and form,” Bora said. “There is a dense, deeply felt emotional layer running through the film, and the film’s unique style becomes a way of expressing that emotion rather than an end in itself. That is exactly the kind of cinema Platoon One wants to stand behind: original, distinctive and deeply rooted voices. I couldn’t let go of this film after I saw it.”

	The brothers divide their time between Mumbai and Delhi. Aakarsh has worked as an assistant director to Reema Kagti, Abhinay Deo and Pushpendra Misra, while Agrim trained as a filmmaker with a focus on editing and assisted editor Deepa Bhatia on “Skater Girl.”

	The pair co-wrote and co-directed their first feature, the experimental “To Caterpillar, From Butterfly,” which debuted at the Dharamshala International Film Festival.

title: The Negative Melted, the Legend Didn’t: Inside the Resurrection of Kamal Amrohi and Meena Kumari’s Storied Indian Epic ‘Pakeezah’
description: On the night of Feb. 3, 1972, the prints of “Pakeezah” arrived at Bombay’s Maratha Mandir cinema in a palanquin pulled by four horses. Military ban
body:
On the night of Feb. 3, 1972, the prints of “Pakeezah” arrived at Bombay’s Maratha Mandir cinema in a palanquin pulled by four horses. Military bands played outside, police held back the thousands crowding the gates, and inside, the film’s star, Meena Kumari, sat beside her husband, director Kamal Amrohi, and gripped his wrist so hard through the screening that her nails drew blood.

	Amrohi’s son Tajdar was in the theater that night. His father never pulled his arm away.
	

	“He just gave a smile, and she also smiled in an embarrassment, you can say,” Tajdar Amrohi says. “And it seems that even after 54 years, I feel as if that incident took place yesterday.”


	Kumari died on March 31, 1972, weeks after the film opened. Now, Film Heritage Foundation’s (FHF) 4K restoration of “Pakeezah,” carried out with the Amrohi family, is back in front of audiences. Thierry Frémaux presents its world premiere at Festival Lumière in Lyon on Wednesday. It then plays a gala at the BFI London Film Festival’s BFI Imax on Oct. 18 that Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, the foundation’s director, will introduce with Tajdar Amrohi, his sister Rukhsar Amrohi and Kamal Amrohi’s grandson Bilal Amrohi. Dungarpur says he heard the Imax screening sold out “in no time.”

	The film is set in Lucknow as the age of the nawabs (Muslim nobles) fades. Kumari plays Sahibjaan, born in a graveyard to a courtesan who was spurned by her husband’s aristocratic family. Raised in a brothel, Sahibjaan grows up to be the most celebrated courtesan of her day, though she longs for love and respectability. Then Salim, a forest officer played by Raaj Kumar, wanders into her train compartment by mistake while she is asleep. Taken with her feet, he leaves her a note in verse and slips away. When they meet again, they fall in love, but the stigma attached to her profession stands between them.
	

	Few Indian films carry a backstory as heavy as this one. Amrohi was already married, with three children, when he married Kumari. Rukhsar grew up with her mother in the family’s hometown of Amroha, in Uttar Pradesh, until she was 13, while her father lived in Bombay (now Mumbai) with Kumari, whom the children called Chhoti Ammi (little mother). Amrohi conceived “Pakeezah” in the mid-1950s around Kumari, his wife and muse, and shooting began in 1956, in black-and-white, before moving to Eastmancolor and then CinemaScope. The production stalled in 1964 when the couple separated, and Kumari’s health declined sharply over the following years. The film’s German cinematographer, Josef Wirsching, who had come with Himansu Rai and Devika Rani from Bombay Talkies, died partway through. Composer Ghulam Mohammed died in 1968 after writing the songs, leaving Naushad to complete the background score.

	Through all of it, Amrohi refused to let the film go.

	“His relations, his health, his wealth – he put everything into ‘Pakeezah,’” his daughter Rukhsar Amrohi says.

	She remembers that every household request, from new decor to things for himself, got the same answer: after “Pakeezah.” His kurtas (tunics), which usually arrived from Lucknow a dozen at a time every six months, wore thin during the shoot. When she pressed him to reorder, he told her that people came to see him, not his clothes.

	“I’ll order all of this after ‘Pakeezah’ – not 12, I’ll get 24 – but let my ‘Pakeezah’ get into theaters,” she recalls him saying.

	Tajdar Amrohi says that by the time the film was ready for release, his father didn’t have a penny to keep for himself and was deep in debt. Financiers, Rukhsar says, pushed him to drop Ghulam Mohammed’s music as old-fashioned and credit Laxmikant-Pyarelal or Shankar-Jaikishan instead. He refused, whether or not that meant the film got made.

	The family’s own life bent around the production. When Kumari left and the shoot stopped, Amrohi sent Rukhsar and her mother back to Amroha. He didn’t want anyone to say that his first wife and daughter had arrived and driven Kumari out. He later wrote to Rukhsar asking her to raise her small hands in prayer that he would finish the picture. He had expected to complete it in a year, and it now felt like a noose around his neck.
	

	“Isn’t that a sacrifice?” she says.

	When shooting resumed, the haveli (mansion) set on Stage 3 at Filmistan Studio in Goregaon was modeled on the Amrohis’ ancestral home in Amroha. Rukhsar went to the set every day because her father wanted her there. She also traveled with the unit to Mysore for the outdoor shoot of the song “Mausam Hai Aashiqana” and the elephant attack sequence. Her mother’s paandaan (a box for paan, or betel leaf), part of her wedding trousseau, was lent at Amrohi’s request. It appears in the Gulabi Mahal (Pink Palace) scenes beside the actor Nadira. It now sits in the drawing room of the Amroha house, which Rukhsar restored and filled with her father’s furniture, photographs and belongings. Locals, she says, began calling it Kamal Amrohi’s museum.

	The siblings are protective of how their father’s marriage is remembered. Tajdar Amrohi is adamant that the couple never divorced, and says that Kumari had asked Amrohi to promise he never would, calling him Chandan, her pet name for him. He also pushes back on the widely told account that actors Sunil Dutt and Nargis and composer Khayyam persuaded Kumari to return to the film in 1969. Dutt deserves credit for going to her, he says, but many others in the industry, Ashok Kumar among them, had urged the same.

	“Frankly speaking, if Meena ji herself hadn’t wanted to complete this film, she wouldn’t have,” he says.

	Nor, he says, did “Pakeezah” become a hit because its star died weeks after release, a reading his sister also rejects. If that were how it worked, he argues, “Every producer-director would pray that once the film is complete, one of their main artists leaves the world, and the film will be a hit. That’s not how it is. A good thing is good, and a bad thing is bad and won’t run.”

	Tajdar Amrohi was at St. Elizabeth Nursing Home on Malabar Hill when Kumari died, and says it was the first time he had ever seen tears in his father’s eyes. Amrohi died in 1993 and is buried beside her. His son sees that as a kind of divine verdict on decades of gossip about the pair.

	“Just as Shah Jahan immortalized Mumtaz Mahal by building the Taj Mahal, Kamal sahab [sir] immortalized Chhoti Ammi, Meena ji, across the whole world by making ‘Pakeezah,’” he says.
	

	For Rukhsar Amrohi, who also calls Kumari Chhoti Ammi, the film is a token of the couple’s love, made by her father out of his love for Kumari. “‘Pakeezah’ is the love child of our Baba [father] and Chhoti Ammi,” she says.

	For Dungarpur, the film goes back to his own childhood. He was 3 when it was released, and his grandmother, Usha Rani, the Maharani (queen) of Dumraon in Bihar, was obsessed with it. She played its LP and later took him to see it on rerelease. He founded FHF in her memory in 2014 and had wanted to restore “Pakeezah” ever since.

	“It’s one of my most beautiful memories of restoration, and the most important film in my life,” he says. “She was the driving force on seeing this restoration.”

	The job turned out to be among the hardest the foundation has taken on. When the FHF team examined the film’s original camera negative at a Mumbai lab, it had melted, with no images left on the celluloid.

	“Meena ji went into a coma two days before her death, and the negative of ‘Pakeezah’ had also gone into a coma,” Tajdar Amrohi says.

	The team rebuilt the film from an interpositive, a CinemaScope print and a color reversal internegative held at the National Film Archive of India, which Dungarpur credits to archivist P.K. Nair. The sound negative had also survived. The two-year restoration was carried out at L’Immagine Ritrovata in Bologna, with the soundtrack remixed in 5.1.

	The on-and-off shoot left its own scars. Day-for-night sequences didn’t match from one stretch of the film to the next. The opticals, meaning the fades and shot changes, drifted in and out of focus. Padma Khanna and other doubles performed some of the dances instead of Kumari, which made the continuity puzzle harder.

	Color was the biggest test. The available versions had faded badly, and accounts differed on whether Kumari’s costume in “Inhi Logon Ne” was pink or red. Original color photographs were scarce, since continuity stills were usually shot in black-and-white to save money. FHF found a few, and Rukhsar Amrohi, who had been on set, came to Dungarpur’s studio to check them. She told him the lyric itself mentions a dupatta (scarf) dyed pink, so red couldn’t be right, and pushed for a deep magenta. That is what made it to the screen.
	

	“You have to make sure that you don’t do something which he had not done, or you enhance it to that level, but keep it exactly his vision, the way he had conceived the film,” Dungarpur says.

	He points viewers to the tracking shot at the end of the “Chalte Chalte” song where the camera glides over a fountain. For him it shows what the film’s camera team pulled off before zoom lenses were in common use. The film also has an anniversary this month: Dungarpur notes that Oct. 8 marked the 100th birthday of its male lead, Raaj Kumar, who replaced an aging Ashok Kumar as Salim.

	FHF has run into missing negatives before. Dungarpur says the restored “Sholay” had the same problem. So did the foundation’s work on “English, August,” which was rebuilt from a single print, and Shaji N. Karun’s Cannes winner “Piravi,” for which only subtitled prints survive.

	“So much money is spent on the production, so much money is spent, but there’s very little money spent on preserving these elements,” he says. “And that’s been quite a tragic story of India’s cinematic history.”

	The foundation has had a busy 12 months on the festival circuit. It took “In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones” to Berlin, “Amma Ariyan” to Cannes and “English, August” to Venice, with stops including New York, Toronto, Shanghai, Singapore and the Festival of Three Continents. Dungarpur says FHF deliberately programs Indian commercial landmarks such as “Sholay,” “Pakeezah” and “Amar Akbar Anthony” next to independent titles. That way, Western audiences who would otherwise never see them get the chance. “Pakeezah” is set to travel to the Smithsonian and the Academy Museum, and its producers plan a wide release in India.

	FHF’s next restorations are Shyam Benegal’s “Bhoomika” and “Mandi,” John Abraham’s “Agraharathil Kazhuthai” (“Donkey in a Brahmin Village”) and Aribam Syam Sharma’s “Imagi Ningthem” (“My Son, My Precious”). The Abraham film will be the foundation’s first Tamil-language restoration. With Criterion, FHF is restoring Bimal Roy’s “Bandini,” “Devdas” and “Madhumati” as well as Satyajit Ray’s “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne,” and it plans to take on “Piravi.”

	Tajdar Amrohi still regrets that “Pakeezah” won no awards. When he once complained about it to his father, the director just smiled.
	

	“You haven’t noticed one thing,” he told his son. “All these people who are coming to watch the picture – that is my award.”

title: Six Flags Stock Drops After Parkgoer's Tragic Death
description:
Six Flags Over Georgia
                          Park’s Stocks Drop After Tragic Roller Coaster D
body:
Six Flags Over Georgia
                          Park’s Stocks Drop After Tragic Roller Coaster Death
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 13, 2026
                            5:33 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Six Flags hasn’t just taken a massive blow to their reputation … their stocks got hit hard after a parkgoer tragically died at their Georgia location.
      
    
            According to Forbes, Six Flags’ stock prices had significantly dropped when the market opened on Tuesday to the lowest level since 2009.
      
    
            The outlet reports prices had dipped under $10 per share at one point … and were still down more than 14% just before the market was closed for the day.
      

      
        
              
    
    
            The drop comes after Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was killed after being ejected from the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            9 roller coasters across 6 of the company's theme parks were shut down after Hassan’s tragic death and the investigation is ongoing.
